title: Troubleshooting ladders, captures, and debug
summary: Match Call-ID, CSeq, Via branch, and To tag, then read captures and IOS debug as themselves.

lessons.title: Match a ladder before you change anything
lessons.summary: A ladder is one dialog only after Call-ID, CSeq, the Via branch, and the To tag agree.
objectives: Match messages that belong to one dialog
Separate a Via branch from a dialog
Say where a 2xx ACK travels

illustration.title: Four fields that tie a ladder
illustration.caption: Read these before you rename a header or change a route.

layers.name: Call-ID
layers.detail: Same value on every hop of this dialog

layers.name: CSeq
layers.detail: Number plus method. ACK uses the INVITE number.

layers.name: Via branch
layers.detail: Identifies one transaction on one hop

layers.name: To tag
layers.detail: Absent on the first request. Present once the dialog exists.

sections.h: Match the dialog, then the transaction
paragraphs: Start with Call-ID. Every request and response in this dialog carries the same Call-ID. CSeq is a number and a method: the INVITE that opened the dialog, the responses to it, and the ACK that completes a 2xx all share that number, while the method token changes. A later re-INVITE uses a higher CSeq number.

The Via branch identifies a single transaction on a single hop. The magic cookie z9hG4bK is how you spot a branch that claims to follow RFC 3261. The To tag is empty on the initial request and present on responses that form the dialog. Matching a response to a request means Call-ID, CSeq, and the Via branch you sent, and then the To tag tells you the dialog exists.

The ACK that follows a 200 OK is end to end. It is its own request, it uses a new Via branch, and it is routed toward the Contact from the 200 OK. RFC 3261 defines that split. RFC 6026 corrects how transactions handle 2xx responses to INVITE, including the ACK that belongs with them.

The ACK that follows a non-2xx final response is hop by hop. It uses the same Via branch as the INVITE it acknowledges, and the previous hop consumes it. When you draw a ladder, label those two ACKs differently. A B2BUA may show you two dialogs; match each leg on its own Call-ID before you decide an ACK is missing.

RFC 3665 is a set of basic call-flow examples. Use it as a shape for the arrows, then trust the headers in the capture you actually have. A clean ladder names the parties, the method or status, and one sentence about why that hop matters.

Change a route, a codec list, or a timer only after the ladder says which hop failed. If Call-ID differs, you are looking at two calls. If the branch differs, you are looking at a new transaction. If the To tag is missing on a response that claims to be in-dialog, the dialog was never formed.

quiz.q: Which field identifies one transaction on one hop?
quiz.why: Call-ID groups the dialog. The branch groups the transaction hop.

choices: End to end, with its own branch
Hop by hop, on the INVITE branch
Only as far as the first proxy
quiz.why: RFC 3261 separates that ACK from the hop-by-hop ACK used for non-2xx finals. RFC 6026 fixes the 2xx transaction handling.

choices: Hop by hop on the INVITE branch
End to end like a 2xx ACK
As a response, not a request
quiz.why: Non-2xx ACKs are part of the INVITE transaction and stop at the next hop.

quiz.q: A To tag on the initial INVITE means
choices: This request is already in a dialog
quiz.why: A To tag on a request means an existing dialog. A brand-new INVITE omits it.

choices: This hop received the INVITE and will retransmit less often
quiz.why: 100 is hop-by-hop and provisional. Ringing is 180.

quiz.q: RFC 3665 is useful here because it
quiz.why: Use it as a picture. The headers in your capture still win.

cards.back: Same value for the dialog. A B2BUA may use a new one on the other leg.
Integer plus method. The ACK for an INVITE keeps the INVITE's number.
Transaction hop id. Look for the z9hG4bK cookie.
End to end. New branch. RFC 6026 corrects the transaction rules around it.

fault.title: Two calls on one screen
fault.symptom: A 200 OK is on the screen and the phone still rings.
fault.log:
INVITE Call-ID: a84b4c76e66710@example.com CSeq: 1 INVITE branch=z9hG4bK7766as01
SIP/2.0 200 OK Call-ID: other-call@example.com CSeq: 1 INVITE branch=z9hG4bK7766as01
choices: The 200 belongs to a different Call-ID
The To tag is optional on every request
fault.why: Call-ID a84b4c76e66710@example.com and Call-ID other-call@example.com are two dialogs.
fault.cause: The success response was matched by branch habit and not by Call-ID.
fault.fix: Pair the 200 to the INVITE only when Call-ID, CSeq, and the Via branch agree. Then look for the end-to-end ACK on that same Call-ID.

lessons.title: Status codes you will actually see
lessons.summary: Read provisional and final codes from RFC 3261 section 21, and keep 422 with RFC 4028.
objectives: Separate provisional codes from final ones
Place 422 with the session-timer RFC
Use 488 for this UA and 606 for a global refusal

illustration.title: Codes for this track
illustration.caption: 422 is Session Interval Too Small from RFC 4028. The other rows are the RFC 3261 section 21 phrases this lesson teaches, plus 606.

paragraphs: 100 Trying is hop by hop and means this hop has the INVITE. 180 Ringing means alerting. 183 Session Progress is the provisional you meet when early media or other progress needs to be signaled before the final answer. None of these three is a final response.

200 OK is the success final response. 302 Moved Temporarily points at a Contact and steps the redirect server out of the dialog. Read the Contact on the 302 and send a new request; the 302 itself is finished once it has been acknowledged as a non-2xx final on that hop.

sections.h: Challenges, busy, cancel, and server errors
paragraphs: 401 Unauthorized is the challenge from a user agent server, commonly a registrar. 407 Proxy Authentication Required is the challenge from a proxy. 408 Request Timeout means the request timed out. 480 Temporarily Unavailable, 486 Busy Here, and 603 Decline are three different refusals: away, busy at this UA, and an explicit decline.

487 Request Terminated is the final response that follows a successful CANCEL of the INVITE. The CANCEL transaction itself completes with 200 OK and CSeq method CANCEL. 500 Server Internal Error and 503 Service Unavailable are server-side failures. 503 often travels with Retry-After. The ACK for every one of these non-2xx finals is hop by hop.

sections.h: 488, 606, and the code that is not in the base list
paragraphs: 488 Not Acceptable Here means this user agent cannot accept the request, often because the session description has no usable overlap. 606 Not Acceptable means the refusal is global: retrying another UA is not expected to help. Keep those two phrases apart when you write the ticket.

422 Session Interval Too Small is defined in RFC 4028, not in the RFC 3261 section 21 list. The response carries Min-SE. The UAC acknowledges the 422 with a hop-by-hop ACK and sends a new INVITE whose session interval is at least that Min-SE. Quoting 422 as a base RFC 3261 status is the mistake this lesson exists to stop.

fault.title: 422 filed as a base status
fault.symptom: A carrier answers Session-Expires: 90 with 422 and Min-SE: 1800. The ticket says RFC 3261 section 21 defines 422.
fault.log:
INVITE CSeq: 1 INVITE
Session-Expires: 90;refresher=uac
SIP/2.0 422 Session Interval Too Small
Min-SE: 1800
CSeq: 1 INVITE
choices: 422 is the session-timer refusal in RFC 4028
422 means the codec list was empty
Min-SE is an RTP sequence number
The hop-by-hop ACK is omitted after 422
fault.why: The reason phrase is Session Interval Too Small. The base section 21 list is the wrong citation.
fault.cause: The offered session interval is below the far end's Min-SE.
fault.fix: ACK the 422 hop by hop, then send a new INVITE whose Session-Expires is at least the Min-SE in the 422. Cite RFC 4028.

lessons.title: Display filters for SIP and RTP
lessons.summary: Filter the capture with sip, rtp, and sip.Method, and confirm sip.CSeq.method in the SIP display-filter reference.
objectives: Use the display filters this lesson names
Confirm a CSeq field in the Wireshark reference
Read Call-ID from the packet you selected

illustration.title: From file to one transaction
illustration.caption: Display filters narrow what you see. They are not a second copy of the SIP RFC.

paragraphs: The display filters you may type from this lesson are sip, rtp, and sip.Method. A common way to see INVITE requests is sip.CSeq.method == "INVITE". Confirm that field in the Wireshark SIP display-filter reference before you trust it in a ticket. The reference for SIP fields is the page this lesson cites as ws-sip. RTP display fields have their own page, ws-rtp.

sip.Method is the safe method field when you want the request method. This lesson does not invent other field names. If a blog names a filter you have not found on those two reference pages, leave it out of the write-up until you confirm it there.

sections.h: What you read after the filter hits
paragraphs: Select one packet and read the SIP headers in order: Call-ID, CSeq, Via branch, To tag. The filter got you to the packet. The match rules from the ladder lesson decide whether the next packet is the same transaction.

rtp shows the media packets. SIP showing a 200 OK with an m= line does not mean those RTP packets are in the capture. When the call is silent, keep the SIP filter long enough to read the negotiated address and port, then use the rtp display filter to see whether media arrived. Cite the RTP reference for RTP fields and the SIP reference for SIP fields.

lessons.title: 488 codecs and 422 session timers
lessons.summary: 488 is this UA refusing the session description. 422 is a session interval below Min-SE.
objectives: Read 488 as an offer/answer refusal at this UA
Retry 422 with a large enough session interval
Keep telephone-event in the overlap you meant to keep

illustration.title: Two finals that look like media failed
illustration.caption: They are different requests to the next INVITE.
rows: This UA rejects the session description
A new offer this UA can accept, or stop
Refusal is global, not just this UA
A different offer, not a different UA hop
New INVITE with Session-Expires at least Min-SE

paragraphs: 488 Not Acceptable Here often means the codec or the rest of the SDP was refused by this user agent. RFC 3261 names the status. RFC 3264 is the offer/answer model: the answer may keep a subset of the offered payloads, and an empty overlap of usable media is a failure. 606 would mean the problem is global rather than local to this UA.

PCMU payload 0 and PCMA payload 8 are static names from RFC 3551. telephone-event is the RFC 4733 name for named telephone events, including DTMF. If the answer keeps PCMU and drops PCMA, the call can still proceed. If the answer has no shared audio codec, expect 488 from this UA instead of a 200 OK.

sections.h: 422 is the timer, not the codec
paragraphs: RFC 4028 defines 422 Session Interval Too Small. The UAS sends Min-SE. A synthetic example in this lesson uses Session-Expires: 90 on the first INVITE and Min-SE: 1800 on the 422. 1800 is an example value for the drill, not a universal carrier rule.

ACK that 422 hop by hop, on the INVITE's Via branch. Then send a new INVITE, new branch, next CSeq, with Session-Expires at least the Min-SE you were given. Leaving the codec list alone is the point: 422 did not say the codecs were unacceptable.
On 488, change the offer. Confirm telephone-event is still there if DTMF has to survive. On 422, change the session interval. Doing both in one new INVITE hides which fix worked.
Early offer puts the SDP in the INVITE. The 200 OK carries the answer. A 488 carries no accepted answer. Read the code before you read a packet capture for RTP that the refusal means will not start.

lessons.title: TLS names, trust anchors, and version
lessons.summary: Handshake failures stay below SIP. A Teams 403 is the Contact FQDN rule after TLS is up.
objectives: Separate handshake failures from SIP status codes
Require TLS 1.2 or newer toward Teams
Put an FQDN in Contact or expect 403

illustration.title: Where the failure sits
illustration.caption: The first three stop before a SIP status. The fourth is SIP.

paragraphs: Certificate name mismatch, an untrusted CA, and a TLS version the peer will not accept all fail in the handshake. You get no SIP status code from the far end, because the SIP message was never delivered. Say handshake in the ticket, and name which of the three you checked.

objectives: Read number, category, and Obsoletes or Updates

layers.name: Category
layers.detail: Standards Track, BCP, Informational, and the rest

layers.name: Obsoletes / Updates
layers.detail: Replacement versus a correction that leaves the base in force

paragraphs: An RFC header gives you the number and the category. RFC 3261 is Standards Track and it is still the base SIP specification. RFC 6881 is the Best Current Practice for emergency calling services. Category is a fact on the header, not a compliment you add in a ticket.

Point at rfc-editor.org for the document you are citing. RFC 5411 is this library's hitchhiker's guide to the SIP specification family. A guide can lag. The header of the specific RFC is the row you quote.

SDP in this library moved from RFC 4566 to RFC 8866. The header on RFC 8866 is where you confirm the Obsoletes line. ICE in this library is RFC 8445, which moved from RFC 5245. STUN in this library is RFC 8489, which moved from RFC 5389. TURN in this library is RFC 8656, which moved from RFC 5766. If a still newer RFC obsoletes one of those and this edition does not cite it, the RFC Editor banner wins.

RFC 6026 corrects transaction handling for 2xx responses to INVITE. Read its header for the Updates line. It is not a replacement of RFC 3261. RFC 4028 is where 422 lives. It is not an Obsoletes of the section 21 list; it is an extension you cite beside the base protocol.
This lesson does not state publication months. The header prints the date. If you need a date in a design record, copy it from rfc-editor.org for that number on the day you looked.

A timeline of a call is still Call-ID and CSeq. A timeline of a specification is number, category, and whether the header says Obsoletes or Updates. Mixing those two timelines is how a ticket cites a blog instead of the document.

paragraphs: Toll fraud here means billable sessions the enterprise did not intend. The four situations you classify are unauthenticated INVITEs from the public internet, digest passwords that are short or shared or still at a vendor default, dial-peers whose destination pattern matches more numbers than the numbering plan, and routes that can complete calls to international destinations outside that plan.

The job in this lesson is to recognize the class and close it. You list the addresses allowed to present signaling, you make each dial-peer match the plan, and you alarm when completions fall outside the plan. The ladder below is a normal call among the lab addresses. It is the path you intend to keep.

Source restrictions mean inbound VoIP signaling is accepted from addresses you listed. In this lab those documentation addresses are 203.0.113.10, 203.0.113.20, 198.51.100.30, and 192.0.2.40. On the border, the usual remote sources are the call agent at 198.51.100.30 and the carrier at 192.0.2.40.

401 and 407 remain the SIP challenges from RFC 3261, with the digest algorithm work in RFC 7616. The secret is operational: unique, long, and stored as a secret. This lesson does not print a password, a hash, or a default.

paragraphs: The FCC call-authentication page is the public context for authenticated caller ID. RFC 8224 is the SIP authenticated-identity specification in this library. Together they describe signing calling identity for the providers who verify it.

Identity and the trusted list answer different questions. STIR speaks to who the calling identity claims to be. The trusted list speaks to which addresses may present VoIP signaling into the PBX. Keep both, and let the CME and SRST pages own the list procedure for those products.

sections.h: The service URN and the BCP
paragraphs: Emergency calling uses the service URN urn:service:sos, defined in RFC 5031. RFC 6881 is the Best Current Practice for communications services in support of emergency calling. The Request-URI on the synthetic INVITE is that URN.

Enterprise SIP has to carry location according to those documents and the current national rules. This lesson does not invent a state PSAP procedure, a PSAP address, or a civic record. The production location value is the one those documents and the national rules describe.

RFC 6442 specifies location conveyance for SIP, including the Geolocation header. The ladder shows Geolocation and Geolocation-Routing so you can see the header names. The cid body is not attached. A real request carries the location by value or by reference the way RFC 6442 specifies.

Read the location as part of the emergency request, on the same Call-ID as the INVITE. A call that reaches an emergency route without location has missed this requirement even if a 100 Trying came back.

The FCC MLTS page covers Kari's Law and RAY BAUM's Act. Kari's Law is the federal direct-dial and notification duty. RAY BAUM's Act is the federal dispatchable-location duty. Use the FCC page for the wording and for any update.

National rules change on that page, not in this lesson. When you design enterprise SIP, the request carries the service URN and the location, and the operator confirms the current FCC MLTS requirements before the design is called done.

paragraphs: RFC 7866 is the session recording protocol. An SBC may fork a session to a recording server, the SRS, acting as the recording client. That fork is a SIP session of its own, with its own Call-ID, beside the call the parties are on.

RFC 7865 is the metadata for that recording session. This lesson does not paste a metadata document. When you need a field, read 7865. The synthetic INVITE below shows the fork toward srs.example.com and stops there.

sections.h: Disclosed use, and the legal line

lessons.summary: RFC 3246 defines the EF PHB. RFC 4594 maps telephony to EF. This lesson does not design a LAN.

illustration.title: What this lesson claims
illustration.caption: Voice media follows the telephony mapping. Signaling is a different service class in RFC 4594, and this table does not assign it a codepoint.

paragraphs: RFC 3246 defines the Expedited Forwarding per-hop behavior. It recommends a codepoint for that PHB. Use the value printed in the RFC when you mark voice media, and say that you took it from RFC 3246.

RFC 4594 is the configuration guideline for DiffServ service classes. In that guidance the telephony service class is mapped to EF. Voice media is the traffic this lesson marks that way. The SIP messages you debug are not the same service class, and this lesson does not assign them a codepoint from memory.

The call ladder ends in RTP on the addresses and ports in SDP. Those RTP packets are what the telephony mapping applies to. A 200 OK does not itself mark packets. The marking is a network behavior on the media path after the answer.

This lesson does not invent a LAN design, a queue depth, a switch policy, or a campus diagram. The operator's approved design is where those decisions live. If the voice is marked EF and still suffers, the next evidence is loss and delay on that path, not a new SIP status code.

lessons.title: Alarms that match the failure
lessons.summary: Alarm on OPTIONS, TLS expiry, 503, recording-session failure, and trusted-list rejects. Each alarm names its document.
objectives: Tie each alarm to one failure class
Use OPTIONS as a liveness signal

illustration.title: Alarm path
illustration.caption: Page someone with the class, the Call-ID if there is one, and the document.

paragraphs: OPTIONS to a trunk that stops answering is a liveness alarm. RFC 3261 section 11 defines OPTIONS. A burst of 503 Service Unavailable is a server-side alarm, often with Retry-After. Certificate expiry and a TLS version below the peer's floor are handshake alarms, and toward Teams that floor is TLS 1.2.

A SIPREC session to the SRS that fails is a recording alarm. Cite RFC 7866 for the session and keep notice and retention on the legal schedule. A trusted-list reject is an operations alarm: confirm the listed addresses against the CME or SRST page for the product, using the lab pair 198.51.100.30 and 192.0.2.40 when this border is the teaching snippet.

A useful page names the class, the synthetic or real identifier you are allowed to share, and the next single check. For a SIP failure include Call-ID and the status code. For a handshake failure say that no SIP status came back, and name mismatch, CA, or version.
Examples in this lesson are synthetic. A customer syslog stays in the customer's system. The alarm text you practice with uses example.com and the documentation addresses only.

paragraphs: A change window starts from a baseline you can name: the last OPTIONS 200, the current trusted-list snippet, or the current codec offer. Write that down in the ticket with the lab addresses you are using.

illustration.title: A row in the glossary

paragraphs: When you meet a term, write the expansion, the role it plays on a ladder, and the document that defines it. SIP, SDP, and RTP stay three rows. An SBC is usually a B2BUA in the sense RFC 7092 taxonomizes, which is a different row from a pure proxy.

Product names go in a separate column. CUCM can hold registrar and call-control duties. CUBE is a B2BUA you configure from the CUBE basic guide. The glossary row still says the role. The logo does not become the definition.

A row without a document waits. This library's cite keys are the allowed pointers. If a neighbor system has no SIP RFC, the row says so, and you cite the vendor series page or you leave the protocol column blank on purpose.
Re-read the row the next time the RFC Editor header moves. SDP's row in this edition says RFC 8866, with RFC 4566 named as the document it moved from. The header is how you update the row later.

CRM is not a SIP element. This lesson does not invent product features for Salesforce or any other CRM. A screen pop may use a Call-ID your contact center already has. The CRM does not authenticate the INVITE, choose the codec, or terminate the carrier trunk.
Unity Connection is a messaging application reached through the call-control platform. It is not the PSTN trunk point. Cite its series page for the product, and keep the trunk on CUBE or CUCM.
When a neighbor has a series page in this library, use that page. When it does not, say the gap. WFM and QM are in the gap on purpose.

paragraphs: CUCM is the call-control registrar and trunk point in this picture. Phones register there. Trunks toward CUBE or a carrier are configured there. Cite the CUCM series page for the product, and cite RFC 3261 for the SIP those trunks speak.

illustration.title: Interview answers, signaling
illustration.caption: The quiz repeats these rows. It does not introduce a new fact.
rows: Call-ID, then the To tag once it exists
End to end. RFC 3261 and RFC 6026.

paragraphs: Interview answer: you tie a dialog together with Call-ID, and you know the dialog exists when the To tag is present. The first INVITE has no To tag. CSeq carries the number and the method, and the ACK for that INVITE keeps the number. Cite RFC 3261 sections 8 and 12.

Interview answer: the Via branch identifies one transaction on one hop. Look for the magic cookie z9hG4bK. A response matches the request when Call-ID, CSeq, and that branch agree. Cite the Via rules in RFC 3261 and the transaction rules in section 17.

Interview answer: the ACK that follows a 200 OK is end to end. It uses its own Via branch and it is aimed at the Contact from the 200. RFC 3261 defines the split. RFC 6026 corrects transaction handling for 2xx responses to INVITE.

Interview answer: the ACK that follows a non-2xx final response, including 487, is hop by hop and reuses the INVITE branch. The previous hop consumes it. If you cannot say which ACK you mean, you are not done with the question.
Interview answer: 100 Trying means this hop has the INVITE. It is not 180 Ringing and it is not the answer. Cite RFC 3261 section 21.

Interview answer: after a successful CANCEL, the CANCEL transaction completes with 200 OK and CSeq method CANCEL, and the INVITE ends with 487 Request Terminated. The ACK for that 487 is the hop-by-hop kind. Cite RFC 3261 section 21 and section 17.

illustration.title: Interview answers, media
illustration.caption: Say the cite with the sentence.
rows: This UA refused the session description

paragraphs: Interview answer: 488 Not Acceptable Here means this user agent cannot accept the request. For media, that is usually the offer/answer overlap: no shared codec, or another part of the SDP this UA rejects. RFC 3261 names the status. RFC 3264 is the offer/answer model. RFC 6337 is the SIP usage of that model.

Interview answer: 606 Not Acceptable means the refusal is global, not local to this UA. Retrying another user agent is not the fix 606 is telling you to try. 488 and 606 are different sentences in a ticket.

Interview answer: 422 Session Interval Too Small is RFC 4028. Read Min-SE, ACK hop by hop, and send a new INVITE with a session interval at least that large. It is not a codec failure and it is not in the RFC 3261 section 21 base list.

Interview answer: telephone-event is how RFC 4733 names telephone events, including DTMF, inside the SDP. RTP, RFC 3550, carries the voice samples. PCMU payload 0 is the static assignment in RFC 3551. SIP does not carry the samples.

sections.h: Keying is a choice you record
paragraphs: Interview answer: SRTP is RFC 3711. The keying choice on an interconnect is SDES, RFC 4568, or DTLS-SRTP, RFC 5764. You record which one the two sides actually use. This lesson does not crown one of them as universal.

Interview answer: if the call connects and stays silent, the signaling may be fine and the RTP is missing. Read c= and m= from the answer, then look for packets. A keying mismatch can look like silence. Name the keying RFC you intended before you rewrite the dial plan.

paragraphs: Interview answer: an SBC is commonly a back-to-back user agent. RFC 7092 is the taxonomy. RFC 5853 collects requirements from SIP session border control deployments. A B2BUA is a user agent server glued to a user agent client, and it may use a new Call-ID on the outbound leg. Match each leg on its own Call-ID before you call an ACK missing.

Interview answer: you do not assume the carrier leg's Call-ID is the phone's Call-ID. Record-Route is how a proxy stays on the path. A B2BUA does not need Record-Route to be in the middle, because it terminated one dialog and opened another. Say which behavior you see in the trace.

sections.h: Where trunks land, and the list
paragraphs: Interview answer: PSTN SIP lands on CUBE or CUCM. UCCX call control is through CUCM. UCCX does not terminate the carrier trunk. Cite cube-basic, cucm, and uccx. CVP SIP, if the design has CVP, comes from that version's guide. Cite cvp and do not recite a memorized comprehensive script.

Interview answer: the IP address trusted list is an IOS voice control, documented on the CME toll-fraud page and, separately, on the SRST trusted-IP page. It is not a SIP status code and not an RFC. The two pages do not share one list size, so you quote neither number as universal. In this lab the border snippet lists 198.51.100.30 and 192.0.2.40.

Interview answer: toward Microsoft Teams Direct Routing, TLS 1.2 or newer is required, and Contact must contain an FQDN or the INVITE draws 403. Cite the OPTIONS and certificate page and the Direct Routing SIP page. The SIP target this curriculum uses is sip.pstnhub.microsoft.com. The plan page is where the Direct Routing design is confirmed.

Interview answer: a handshake failure, name mismatch, untrusted CA, or old TLS, produces no SIP status. A 403 means SIP arrived and Contact failed the FQDN rule. Those are two answers. Do not merge them.

lessons.title: When the RFC number moves
lessons.summary: SDP, ICE, STUN, and TURN moved. The RFC Editor banner beats a blog, and an uncited successor stays an open question.
objectives: Name the four moves this edition teaches
Read Obsoletes on the header
Mark a possible newer RFC this library does not cite

illustration.title: Moves this edition will say out loud
illustration.caption: Confirm each Obsoletes line on rfc-editor.org. A later banner outranks this table.

paragraphs: SDP moved from RFC 4566 to RFC 8866. ICE moved from RFC 5245 to RFC 8445. STUN moved from RFC 5389 to RFC 8489. TURN moved from RFC 5766 to RFC 8656. This library can cite 4566, 8866, 8445, 8489, and 8656. The older ICE, STUN, and TURN numbers are named here so you can read the Obsoletes line. They are not cite keys in this edition.

The header on the new RFC is where Obsoletes is printed. The old RFC's page is where Obsoleted by is printed. Copy the word that is there. A blog that still teaches RFC 4566 as the current SDP specification loses to the RFC Editor banner.

sections.h: What did not move in that sentence
paragraphs: SIP itself remains RFC 3261. RFC 6026 updates 2xx transaction handling and does not obsolete the base specification. Read Updates versus Obsoletes. Offer/answer remains RFC 3264. RTP remains RFC 3550. Those numbers are current in this library, and you still check their banners.
422 stays RFC 4028. Emergency calling stays RFC 6881, which is a BCP. Recording stays RFC 7866 and RFC 7865. A move in the SDP family is not a move in those documents.

sections.h: Uncertainty you are required to keep
paragraphs: A successor might exist that this edition does not cite. If the RFC Editor page for 8866, 8445, 8489, or 8656 shows a newer obsoleting document, that banner wins and this table is stale. This lesson does not claim these four numbers are permanent.

RFC 5411 can help you find the SIP family and can itself be older than the header you need. Publication months are not stated here. When a design record needs a date, copy it from the header on the day you looked.

fault.title: A frozen number
fault.symptom: A design freezes SDP as RFC 4566 and ICE as RFC 5245, and it says the table in class cannot be wrong even if the RFC Editor shows a newer document.
fault.log:
Design (synthetic): SDP RFC 4566 current. ICE RFC 5245 current.
Banner check refused.
choices: Cite RFC 8866 and RFC 8445, and accept a still newer banner if one exists.
Invent publication months to settle it
fault.why: This edition's current numbers are 8866 and 8445. An uncited successor on the banner still wins.
fault.cause: The class table was treated as permanent.
fault.fix: Open rfc-editor.org for those numbers. Write Obsoletes as printed. If the banner names a newer RFC, cite that and mark this lesson's table stale.
